title: Commissioners question police conduct following officer-involved shooting in Forest Lawn
subtitle: Members of Calgary's Sudanese community have said race played a factor in his death, saying that it's less likely he'd have been killed if he was white
article: Questions were raised Wednesday by the city's police commission about systemic shortfalls in the Calgary Police Service's approach to armed suspects following the fatal shooting of a Black man in Forest Lawn last weekend.

In one heated exchange, commissioner Heather Campbell asked why police in Ottawa were able to subdue a menacing Freedom Convoy crowd of thousands with no fatalities while at the same time officers in Calgary couldn't do likewise with a solitary Latjor Tuel.
Tuel was shot multiple times Saturday when he allegedly lunged at officers and a police dog with a knife on 17th Avenue S.E.

It's been suggested he was suffering from a mental-health episode.

"How is it we saw in Ottawa for three weeks people who outnumbered the police, who openly assaulted others, who were armed, unmasked, had weapons both visible and concealed, and police, including members of CPS thankfully, were able to bring the demonstration to conclusion without the discharge of a service weapon," Campbell said to CPS Chief Mark Neufeld.
"How do we explain to the public how that approach was used to de-escalate with the Ottawa blockaders and appeared not to be used with the late Mr. Tuel?"
In reply, Neufeld said the two situations were very different and challenged Campbell to point out any crucial similarities.
"Are you aware in Ottawa of any individual charging toward the police officers with a knife?" he said.
"I don't know the utility of trying to shoehorn this situation with the Ottawa context."
Campbell said she couldn't cite a similar knife-wielding incident in Ottawa but insisted the virtually simultaneous optics were troubling.
"It's not an exercise in futility, chief, it's an exercise in seeking to put it in a perspective a regular Calgarian can understand and why the two situations can't be compared," she said.

Coun. Courtney Walcott, who sits on the commission, said systemic issues of racism and bias that have plagued the CPS and other agencies for many years can't be dismissed as a factor in Saturday's shooting.

"There are gaps that have been clear outside this particular situation that had they been addressed in other ones, it is a fair assumption to suggest that it's possible we could have had a different outcome resulting from the interaction we saw on the weekend," he said.
Neufeld, who acknowledged in 2020 that systemic racism exists in the CPS , said there's still work to be done on that count but that his members can't address mental-health issues alone.

"We did make the commitments and we talked about anti-racism and filling the gaps in crisis response system - it feels like some days, we're the ones doing the lifting and all of a sudden when an incident that happens, it feels like the blame is on the police," said Neufeld.
"There has to be opportunities to keep people out of crisis so these things don't have to get dealt with on 17th Avenue S.E., because that's a bad place to deal with them."
Commissioners critical of police conduct in the shooting "without knowledge or facts" are inflaming the situation, said John Orr, president of the Calgary Police Association.
"This fanning of the flames does nothing to help the community heal and only lends itself to further dividing the police and community they serve - maybe that is their intention," said Orr.
Police say they responded to reports of an assault on 17th Avenue near 44th Street S.E. and confronted Tuel, who rebuffed their verbal attempts to resolve the situation.
They said their use of a Taser and less-lethal baton rounds failed to have much effect, and when Tuel attacked a police dog with a knife, he was fatally shot by two officers.
A video posted on social media shows Tuel sitting on the sidewalk near a bus shelter holding what looked like a walking stick and a knife shortly before he was killed.
One officer held a barking police dog by a leash while another pointed a weapon at the man who appeared to be in a contemplative mood, rising to his feet before kneeling on one knee.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), which is investigating the circumstances of the shooting, said when Tuel advanced toward officers, the dog was allowed to run toward him.
"Video shows that the dog's handler pulled the dog back, upon which the man advanced in the direction of the dog and the handler," said ASIRT.
Tuel then allegedly swung the stick and stabbed the knife at the dog while the dog bit him, said the agency.
After Tuel was shot, he was pronounced dead at the scene.
The animal, known as police service dog Jack, was injured and received emergency veterinary care before being released from hospital Tuesday.
Police arrived at the scene with no knowledge it involved a possible mental-health issue, Neufeld has said.

Those who knew Tuel described him as a loving man who worked to send money to family in South Sudan, where he was forced to serve as a child soldier decades ago - experiences that led to struggles with post-traumatic stress syndrome.
Members of Calgary's Sudanese community have suggested race played a factor in his death, saying that it's less likely he'd have been killed if he was white.
While there may be overall systemic issues at play, the actions of officers on Saturday weren't racist, Neufeld said Wednesday.
"In the manner that they responded, it did not have anything to do with the colour of their skin," he said.
Disinformation in regular and social media have inflamed emotions into believing the shooting was racist, added Neufeld.
With its heavy workload and shortage of resources, Neufeld said it could take up to two years for ASIRT to complete its investigation into the incident.
Meanwhile, a GofundMe page set up to pay for Tuel's funeral and other expenses had raised more than $73,000.
